published_title: NVIDIA After Huang: Can Record Earnings Settle the AI Market’s Nerves?
script_edits:
### SEGMENT 1 — OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol for work, coding, and
ALEX: OpenAI just shipped two new frontier models — not as a research preview, into actual production tools you can use today. GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Live in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API as of yesterday.
JAMIE: Two models. With names. I have so many questions.
RUFUS: I have one. Which one costs more.
### SEGMENT 1 — NVIDIA Earnings After Huang
ALEX: NVIDIA just reported a hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars in quarterly revenue. But after Jensen Huang, who sets its direction?
JAMIE: A huge quarter answers the demand question. It does not answer the leadership question.
RUFUS: Quite. A very large engine still requires someone to choose the destination.
NVIDIA reported earnings yesterday, November eighteenth
NVIDIA reported earnings yesterday, November seventeenth
Picture a midtown Manhattan trading desk at nine-thirty yesterday morning
Picture an imagined midtown Manhattan trading desk after yesterday’s earnings release
After the closing bell, NVIDIA reported earnings

### SEGMENT 2 — Story 1: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol for work, coding
ALEX: Okay. November seventeenth. OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol — both live right now in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API. Astra for demanding reasoning and coding, Sol for everyday coding and agent workflows. So: two models. Is that twice as useful or twice the headache?
JAMIE: My first instinct was "not again with the naming." But the split actually makes sense to me.
ALEX: Walk me through it.
JAMIE: If you're writing something complex — multi-step reasoning, tricky architecture — you want the heaviest model available. But if you're automating repetitive tasks or spinning up agents, you don't need that. Sol exists so you're not paying for a sledgehammer to tap a nail.
ALEX: Rufus, you made a face when I said "API."
RUFUS: I was calculating. It's a reflex.
ALEX: And?
RUFUS: The split creates a decision point. Every time you build something, you have to ask: Astra problem or Sol problem? That's choosing inference cost — the price per request — every time you make an architectural decision. The overhead isn't zero.
JAMIE: But that's already the world we live in. GPT-4o, o1, whatever came before. Developers are used to picking the right tool.
RUFUS: They are. I'm just noting it adds up.
ALEX: So the real question is whether the specialization saves you enough time and money to justify the choosing.
JAMIE: For coding specifically, I think yes. Picture you're in Codex — OpenAI's coding environment — and your day splits into two buckets: hard architectural problems and boilerplate. The boilerplate is probably seventy percent of your day.
ALEX: Boilerplate being the repetitive structural code every project needs but isn't the interesting part.
JAMIE: The scaffolding. If Sol handles that reliably, your senior engineers are actually solving problems instead of writing the same setup code for the fourth time this month.
RUFUS: The sleeper in this announcement, to me, is tool calling through the Responses API.
ALEX: Explain that for people who haven't touched the API.
RUFUS: Tool calling means the model can reach out and use external software — run a search, check a database, trigger another process. The Responses API is OpenAI's newer framework that enables it. What's notable is that tool calling is only available through Responses, not through the older Chat Completions pathway.
ALEX: So if you want your agent to actually do things, rather than just describe doing things, you need the newer plumbing.
RUFUS: Which means any team still on the older integration has to migrate before they get the full capability.
JAMIE: That's not nothing for a larger company.
RUFUS: No. But it's a migration with a clear destination, not a wall.
ALEX: OpenAI also shipped updated safety materials with this release — tighter restrictions specifically around higher-risk cybersecurity use.
JAMIE: The timing is interesting. You're releasing your most capable coding models and simultaneously saying: here's where the ceiling is for security research. I find it notable that the documentation arrived with the models rather than a month after.
ALEX: Reassuring or just paperwork?
ALEX: One thing I keep turning over — Sol is for agent workflows, right? But agents need to call tools. And tool calling requires the Responses API. So if you pick Sol specifically because you want agents, you've already committed to the newer framework. The choice makes the migration.
JAMIE: Oh, that's actually a tighter constraint than it sounds. You don't just choose a model. You choose a whole plumbing stack at the same time.
RUFUS: Which is either elegant design or a very effective way to move developers off the older pathway.
ALEX: Maybe both.
JAMIE: Probably both.
RUFUS: What I haven't seen answered is whether the safety restrictions — the tightened cybersecurity ceiling — apply equally to Astra and Sol, or whether Astra gets a stricter ceiling because it's the more capable model.
ALEX: OpenAI's documentation doesn't distinguish between the two on that point, as far as we have it.
JAMIE: So a security researcher using Sol for what they'd call routine analysis doesn't know if they're inside the boundary or not.
RUFUS: That's a genuinely open question. And the kind of thing where "read the documentation" is correct advice that also isn't fully sufficient yet.
ALEX: Noted. Test the models, check your API pathway, and apparently also read the fine print on cybersecurity use before your security team touches either one.
RUFUS: Cheerful morning listening.
JAMIE: We're helpful that way.
JAMIE: One thing I'd actually push back on slightly — the split assumes developers can predict which bucket a problem falls into before they start. Some of the most expensive tasks start as boilerplate and turn into architectural problems halfway through.
RUFUS: That's a fair constraint. Though you could argue it's also recoverable — you route mid-task to Astra if Sol hits its ceiling. The API lets you switch.
ALEX: Is that how it works in practice, or is that the ideal?
RUFUS: We don't have real-world data on that yet. What we have is OpenAI's framing and the architecture. The performance delta between the two on actual developer work — that's the number this community will fill in over the next few weeks.
JAMIE: Which is why the honest advice is: test on your own work, not someone else's benchmark.
ALEX: Both models are in ChatGPT Work and Codex now. And if you're on the API, check whether you're using Responses or Chat Completions — that one detail determines whether tool calling is available to you at all.
RUFUS: Possibly the most load-bearing sentence in this whole story.
JAMIE: And the least glamorous.
### SEGMENT 3 — Story 2: NVIDIA Posts Strong Earnings Amid Leadership Transition
ALEX: Our second story. NVIDIA reported earnings yesterday, November seventeenth — first report since Jensen Huang left. Interim CEO Colette Kress ran the call. And they beat analyst expectations.
JAMIE: I genuinely did not expect that headline.
ALEX: The lead was: everything is fine. Markets responded accordingly. But.
RUFUS: There is always a but.
ALEX: Rufus, take us on location.
RUFUS: Picture an imagined midtown Manhattan trading desk after yesterday’s earnings release — three screens, cold coffee, someone eating a sandwich while watching a ticker. After the closing bell, NVIDIA reported earnings that cleared analyst targets. Colette Kress ran the call, emphasised continuity, and the market exhaled. Not just NVIDIA — AMD up, Broadcom up. The whole AI hardware sector moved.
JAMIE: Which tells you something about where the anxiety actually was.
RUFUS: The market wasn't pricing in collapse. It was pricing in uncertainty. The earnings removed the uncertainty. So the rally isn't celebrating strong results so much as a collective deep breath. The question everyone had been sitting with was: without Jensen Huang, does this machine keep running? Yesterday's answer was — for now, yes.
JAMIE: "For now, yes" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, Rufus.
RUFUS: It is. Reuters also noted that investors remain concerned about a potential SEC probe. That hasn't resolved. So you have a company that beat on earnings, steadied its supply-chain partners, and still has a legal overhang nobody can price with any precision.
ALEX: Back to the wider story. Jamie, you were asking about culture before we went to Rufus. What's your read?
JAMIE: NVIDIA was Jensen Huang's company in a way that's genuinely unusual even for tech. His tenure, his personal conviction on GPU strategy, the way the company became load-bearing infrastructure for AI — that's not a standard CEO relationship. And now Colette Kress, who was CFO, is the one on the earnings call.
JAMIE: That is a very different communication style and a very different signal.
ALEX: Different good or different bad?
JAMIE: Different appropriate-for-the-moment, maybe. CFOs are built for stability messaging, and stability is exactly what the room needed yesterday. But what NVIDIA has to do next — where it invests, what it builds for the next GPU generation, how it answers AMD and the custom silicon that hyperscalers are quietly developing in-house —
JAMIE: those are strategic bets that need a vision, not a steady hand on the quarterly numbers.
RUFUS: And the earnings call gave us no evidence of who is making those bets.
ALEX: Right. It confirms the company is running. It doesn't tell you where it's running to.
RUFUS: The AMD move is worth unpacking though. If you're a buyer nervous about NVIDIA's supply chain, you start hedging toward AMD — that's rational. But if NVIDIA stabilises, the hedging pressure relieves and that bump could unwind quickly.
JAMIE: Or buyers have been diversifying for eighteen months already and this just made it legible.
RUFUS: Heh. That is the more troubling reading for NVIDIA, yes.
ALEX: The SEC investigation — Reuters flagged it, but it's still vague. Scope unknown, timeline unknown.
RUFUS: Which is the honest position. We have strong earnings, a known unknown on the legal side, and an open question on strategic direction. Three different clocks running at three different speeds.
ALEX: So practically: if you have NVIDIA hardware in your infrastructure or your portfolio, the number to watch isn't the stock price — it's chip supply lead times. Earnings say the company is healthy. Lead times will tell you if the actual product is still moving through the pipeline.
JAMIE: And if you're an IT buyer who's been stalling a procurement decision — the leadership transition alone probably isn't reason enough to pause. The operational side looks intact.
RUFUS: I would keep one eye on the SEC situation. That's the variable nobody can read yet, including the market.
ALEX: Agreed. Lead times, the investigation, and whoever they name as permanent CEO — that appointment will say more about NVIDIA's next chapter than any earnings call.
JAMIE: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Alex, if everything is breaking news, when are we supposed to get any work done?
ALEX: That's the question The Ledger helps you work through: five focused briefings connecting AI news with the decisions in front of you.
RUFUS: The Ledger. Because reading another headline is a marvellous way to postpone deciding anything. I admire the efficiency of the procrastination.
JAMIE: Rufus has diagnosed the problem. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Back to the story.
